› Without running any commands, write about 300 words explaining how a terminal emulator
  turns a byte stream into a cell grid. Use two short paragraphs and a short bulleted list.


• A terminal emulator receives a byte stream from a program through a pseudoterminal (PTY). It
  first decodes ordinary bytes into characters using an encoding such as UTF-8, but not every
  byte represents visible text. Control characters and escape sequences act as instructions:
  move the cursor, erase part of the screen, change colors, enable bold text, switch to an
  alternate screen, or set a scrolling region. Because these instructions can arrive across
  multiple reads, the emulator uses a stateful parser. It may retain an incomplete UTF-8
  character or escape sequence until later bytes complete it. Unsupported or malformed
  sequences are handled according to the emulator’s compatibility rules.

  The parsed operations update an in-memory model of the terminal screen. This model is
  usually a rectangular grid of cells, with each cell storing a character or grapheme, styling
  attributes, and sometimes metadata such as hyperlink information. Printable text is placed
  at the cursor, which advances according to character width. Most characters occupy one cell,
  East Asian wide characters commonly occupy two, and combining marks modify an existing cell
  rather than consuming another. When text reaches the right edge, wrapping rules determine
  whether the cursor continues on the next row. Writing past the bottom of a scrolling region
  shifts rows upward, often preserving displaced lines in scrollback. The emulator then
  renders changed cells using a font system and graphics API; rendering is separate from
  parsing, so many incoming operations can be combined into one visual update.

  - Input: Read bytes from the PTY.
